title: Interview with a Literary Translator
description: Four recordings about the art, craft and future of translating novels, from an interview to a documentary.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer (A, B, C or D) for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A radio interview
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter, Nam, interviewing a translator called Claire.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Welcome to Book Hour. My guest today is Claire Dunmore, who has translated more than twenty novels from Portuguese into English. Claire, most readers never think about the translator. Does that bother you?

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: Well, it used to, I suppose. When I started, I felt rather invisible. But I've come to see it differently. If I do my job well, the reader forgets I'm there, and that's actually the highest compliment I could receive.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: How did you get into translation? Was it a childhood dream?

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: Not at all. I wanted to be a pianist, believe it or not. I studied music for years, but my hands simply weren't good enough. Then I spent a year in Lisbon working in a bookshop, and I started reading in Portuguese for pleasure. One evening I tried to render a short story into English, just for fun, and I lost the entire night to it.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: And that was it?

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: Not quite. I sent the story to a small magazine, expecting nothing, and they published it. Though to be honest, it took another six years before anyone paid me properly. I worked as a proofreader during the day and translated at night.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Many people assume translation is mostly about vocabulary. Is that fair?

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: It's the least of it, really. Any dictionary can give you words. What's hard is rhythm and tone. A sentence can be perfectly accurate and still sound dead on the page, and then I've failed the author, even though I haven't made a single mistake.

parts.title: Part 2 · A university lecture
parts.intro: You will hear a lecturer, Dr Owen, talking to translation students about equivalence.

script.speaker: Dr Owen
script.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at what translators call the problem of equivalence, and I'll begin by challenging a popular myth, namely that some words are simply untranslatable.

script.speaker: Dr Owen
script.text: Take the Portuguese word saudade, which is often described as impossible to render in English. In fact, translators have managed it many times. They just don't do it with a single word. They use a phrase, or they let the surrounding scene carry the feeling. So the real issue is not possibility, but economy.

script.speaker: Dr Owen
script.text: A much more stubborn problem is humour. Jokes depend on sound, on double meanings, on shared assumptions. If a pun works only because two words happen to sound alike in the original, you cannot carry it across. Translators therefore have to decide whether to explain the joke, which kills it, or to invent a different one that does a similar job.

script.speaker: Dr Owen
script.text: Most professionals choose the second option, and it's a decision that divides the field. Purists argue that inventing a joke betrays the author. I take the opposite view. If the joke makes the reader laugh at the same moment in the story, then the author's intention has been honoured, even though the words have changed.

script.speaker: Dr Owen
script.text: Dialect raises similar questions. Suppose a character speaks in the accent of a poor rural region. Should the translator choose an English regional accent? That risks making a farmer from the Portuguese countryside sound as though he lives in Yorkshire, which is absurd. Most translators now prefer a lighter touch, using rhythm and word order to suggest speech without pointing to a real place.

script.speaker: Dr Owen
script.text: I'd like you to read the two extracts on the handout, then, for next week, write a short commentary explaining which approach you prefer and why. Please don't simply say which version you like. I want evidence from the text.

parts.title: Part 3 · A discussion about machine translation
parts.intro: You will hear a publisher, Mai, and a linguist, Hugh, discussing whether software will replace literary translators.

script.speaker: Hugh
script.text: I'll be provocative, Mai. For ordinary business text, machines already do the job well enough that nobody pays a human. I see no reason why fiction should be immune forever.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Forever is a big word. I'd concede that for instruction manuals you're right. But a novel isn't information. It's a voice. And so far, the machine versions I've seen are smooth but flat, as if every character had been sanded down to the same pleasant tone.

script.speaker: Hugh
script.text: Smooth is an improvement, though. Five years ago they weren't even smooth. Isn't it likely that the flatness will be solved the way the grammar was?

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Possibly, but there's a difference. Grammar has right and wrong answers; style doesn't. Someone has to decide what the book should sound like, and that is a judgement, not a calculation. Publishers will still need a person to take responsibility for that judgement.

script.speaker: Hugh
script.text: Fair point, yet I suspect the role will change rather than vanish. Translators may end up editing machine drafts, rather like pilots monitoring automatic systems.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: That worries me, actually. Editing a draft makes you cautious. You tend to fix errors rather than rethink the whole sentence, and the result drifts towards the safe and the predictable. Readers would notice eventually, I think, even if they couldn't say why.

script.speaker: Hugh
script.text: Perhaps. I'd still say the economics will be decisive, not the art. If a publisher can save half the cost, many will take the risk, particularly with books they expect to sell modestly.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: And that's where we agree, oddly enough. The books at risk are the quiet, unfashionable ones, which are often the most interesting. That's what I'd hate to lose.

parts.title: Part 4 · A documentary
parts.intro: You will hear part of a radio documentary about a retreat for translators.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: In a quiet village on the coast, a small house hosts something unusual: a residential centre for literary translators. Every summer, twelve translators from as many languages arrive for a month, and they do something rarely done in this profession. They work together.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Translation is traditionally lonely. A translator might spend a year with one book and speak to nobody about it except an editor, who may not read the original language. At the centre, each person reads a page aloud in the evening, and the others, who often know nothing of the source language, simply listen for what sounds wrong.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Strangely, that is often enough. A phrase that seems fine on the page can sound clumsy to the ear, and the translator, who has been staring at the original for months, suddenly hears what a stranger would hear.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: The centre was founded by a retired teacher, who had noticed that many of the best translators she knew had given up. Not because of poor reviews, but because of poor pay and long isolation. Her aim was modest: to give them a month where the work felt like a pleasure again. Funding has never been generous; the kitchen is run by volunteers, and the rooms are plain.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Yet the waiting list is now three years long. Past visitors say that what they take away is less a finished chapter than confidence. One of them described it as remembering that you are part of a tradition that is older than any single language.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Critics sometimes ask whether such a place is a luxury. The organisers reply that literature depends on translation, since most readers will only ever meet the world's great books in a language other than the one they were written in. If the translators are exhausted, they argue, everyone eventually pays the price.
